title: Garden Egg Abomu
author: Berlinda Entsie
desc: Garden eggs quartered without cutting through, steamed, mashed in a mortar — and the cue is the bubbles reducing as the oil forms a surface layer.
longDesc: The garden egg version of abomu, from the same author, and it carries two things the other does not. The cutting instruction is precise: quarter the garden eggs with two lengthwise cuts that do not go all the way through, so they hold together while steaming and give up their water. And the finishing cue is the best in either recipe — after the palm oil goes in, watch for the bubbles reducing as the oil forms a surface layer. She is also explicit that mashing must be done in a mortar, because blending will not yield the same texture.
ingredients: 15 small garden eggs, or 8 large ones
5 kpakposhito (pettie belle chilli), or preferred chilli
A piece of koobi (salted dry tilapia)
1 ladle palm oil — see the note on the unit
Sardines, grilled mackerel, fried fish or eggs
equipment: Steamer or pot with a lid
steps: Cut the garden eggs in quarters — two lengthwise cuts, not all the way through.
Steam them with the tomatoes, onion, pepper and koobi until tender, keeping the water.
Mash in a mortar. Blending will not yield the same texture.
Heat the mixture and add the palm oil.
Watch for the bubbles reducing as the oil forms a surface layer.
Fold in your chosen protein and serve.
chefTips: The quartering instruction matters: two lengthwise cuts that stop short of going through. The garden egg opens up to steam but stays in one piece, so it does not waterlog.
Bubbles reducing as the oil forms a surface layer is the finishing cue, and it is the clearest endpoint in either abomu recipe. Before that the water has not cooked off.
Mortar, not blender. Her own words are that blending will not yield the same texture, and she is right — the fibre needs crushing rather than cutting.
Keep the steaming water. It goes back in and carries the flavour of the koobi and the garden eggs.
A ladle of palm oil is not a standard measure and no conversion is offered. Start with two tablespoons and judge by the surface layer.
Fifteen small garden eggs or eight large — the source gives both, and the small ones are more bitter and more flavourful.
The protein is a free choice: sardines, grilled mackerel, fried fish or eggs. That flexibility is how the dish is actually eaten.
commonMistakes: Cutting the garden eggs all the way through.
Adding the oil and serving immediately, before the bubbles subside.
Salting before tasting, when the koobi and stock cubes are both salty.
sources: Adapted from 'DIY Recipes: How to make the best Ghanaian Garden egg Abomu (stew)', pulse.com.gh. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Berlinda Entsie, 11:40 - 10 August 2021'. DATE FLAG: the URL timestamp reads 2024-08-13, disagreeing with the printed date. Both recorded.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 medium-size onion; 5 Kpakposhito (Pettie Belle Chilli) or preferred chili; 2 medium-sized fresh tomatoes; Piece of Koobi (salted dry tilapia); 15 small garden eggs or 8 large ones; 2 Maggie cubes; Sardines/Grilled Mackerel/Fried Fish/eggs (protein choice); Salt; 1 ladle of Palm Oil.

NON-STANDARD UNIT, flagged and NOT converted: '1 ladle of Palm Oil'. A ladle is not a defined measure and varies widely. No figure has been substituted; the tip above offers two tablespoons as a starting point and says so explicitly.
'Piece of Koobi' is likewise unquantified and has not been assigned a weight.
THE CUTTING INSTRUCTION, as printed: cut the garden eggs in quarters with two lengthwise cuts, NOT through. This is a real technique and it is documented nowhere else in the garden egg record.
THE FINISHING CUE, verbatim and the best endpoint in either abomu version: 'Watch for bubbles reducing as oil forms surface layer.'
THE MASHING INSTRUCTION, verbatim: mash in a mortar, because 'blending won't yield same texture'. That is an explicit rejection of the blender, from the author.

Method as printed: quarter the garden eggs; steam with tomatoes, onion, pepper and koobi until tender, KEEPING THE WATER; mash in a mortar; add crushed stock cubes; heat the mixture and add palm oil; watch for the bubble cue.

THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ABOMU AND GARDEN EGG STEW IS NOT SETTLED by any source. This dish shares its main vegetable with GHA026 and GHA027 but its method — steam, mash in earthenware or a mortar, finish with hot palm oil — is the abomu method of GHA028. The author's own definition of abomu, quoted at GHA028, describes a vessel and a technique rather than a set of ingredients, which is how both are filed here.
A THIRD SOURCE under a related name, recorded not published: the Tasty Tom Cookbook's 'Kontomire Abom Sauce', a corporate brand cookbook with no individual author — see the sources at GHA023.
A LEAD NOT RETRIEVED: Adom Online's 'How to prepare Abomu' returned a fetch error, so nothing was taken from it.
reheating: Warm gently, or serve at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Garden eggs are high in fibre, folate and polyphenols, and the small bitter ones most of all.
Koobi and the chosen fish both supply protein, iodine and calcium.
Red palm oil provides provitamin-A carotenoids.
culturalNote: Two abomu recipes from one writer — one of cocoyam leaves, one of garden eggs — make clear that abomu is a way of cooking rather than a particular dish: steam, mash in earthenware, finish with hot palm oil, eat from the bowl. The bubble cue is the sort of thing a cook watches for without ever naming, and it is worth having written down.
